stimulus.text: Paraphrase: From 1934 to 1937, Senator Gerald Nye of North Dakota chaired a Senate committee that investigated whether arms makers and bankers had pushed the United States into World War I. The committee found no proof that these so-called merchants of death had maneuvered the country into war, but its hearings fed the belief that profits had driven the 1917 decision. Congress then passed three Neutrality Acts: the 1935 act banned arms sales to warring nations; the 1936 act banned loans to them; the 1937 act let warring nations buy non-military goods only if they paid cash and carried the goods away in their own ships, a rule called cash-and-carry.

stem: What did the Neutrality Act of 1935 require the United States to do when war broke out abroad?

options.text: Send troops to defend the victim of aggression
options.misconception: The act was meant to keep America out, not to send troops in.

options.text: Lend money to the side defending democracy
options.misconception: Loans to belligerents were banned by the 1936 act.

options.text: Join the League of Nations to stop the war
options.misconception: The United States never joined the League.

options.text: Refuse to sell arms to any warring nation

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Neutrality Acts aimed to keep the United States out of war, not to send troops.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the 1936 Neutrality Act banned loans to belligerents.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the United States stayed out of the League of Nations.
rationales.D: The 1935 act imposed an arms embargo on every belligerent alike.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says the 1935 act banned arms sales to warring nations.
2. The ban applied to every side alike, on the theory that impartiality would keep America out.
3. The aim was to avoid repeating 1917, when trade and loans had tied America to the Allies.
4. Later acts added a ban on loans in 1936 and cash-and-carry in 1937.
Remember: an embargo on everyone is the signature of 1930s neutrality.
